title: Minor Burns & Scalds (First Aid)
scenario: Accidental contact with hot utensils, boiling water, tea, or cooking steam causing red, painful skin.
steps: Immediately cool the burn under gentle, clean running tap water for at least 10 to 20 minutes.
Gently remove tight clothing, bangles, or jewelry near the injured area before swelling starts.
Do NOT break blisters. Leave skin intact to prevent deep bacterial infection.
Cover the area loosely with a clean, dry, lint-free cloth or sterile plastic cling film.
Keep the patient calm and offer sips of clean water if they are fully conscious.
what_not_to_do: NEVER apply ice directly to the burn (causes tissue frostbite).
NEVER apply home remedies like toothpaste, cow dung, ghee, turmeric, ink, or raw eggs.
NEVER forcefully peel off clothing that is stuck directly to burned flesh.
red_flags: Burn area is larger than the palm of the patient's hand.
Burn involves the face, hands, feet, groin, or major joints.
Skin appears charred white, brown, or leathery and painless (Third-degree deep burn).
Patient is an infant under 1 year or an elderly person.
Burn was caused by chemical or high-voltage electrical contact.
doctor_referral_advice: 🚨 If ANY red flag is present, immediately arrange referral to PHC or CHC. Administer oral fluids only if conscious and transfer quickly.
source_citation: MoHFW First Aid Guidelines / WHO Thermal Injury Management

title: Dehydration & Loose Stools (ORS & Zinc Management)
scenario: Passing loose, watery stools 3 or more times a day in children or adults without blood.
steps: Assess hydration status: check thirst, tears, alertness, and skin pinch elasticity.
Prepare clean ORS: Dissolve 1 whole standard ORS packet (20.5 g) in exactly 1 Liter of clean drinking water.
Give small, frequent sips: For children <2 years give 50-100 ml after each loose stool; >2 years give 100-200 ml.
For infants: Continue exclusive and frequent breastfeeding. Do NOT stop breastmilk.
Initiate Zinc supplementation: 10 mg/day for infants 2-6 months; 20 mg/day for children 6-59 months for 14 continuous days.
Continue age-appropriate nutritious feeding (khichdi, mashed banana, curd, dal water).
what_not_to_do: NEVER mix ORS with milk, fruit juices, or commercial sweetened soft drinks.
NEVER boil prepared ORS solution. Use within 24 hours of mixing, then discard.
NEVER give antimotility drugs (like loperamide) to infants or young children.
red_flags: Skin pinch on abdomen goes back very slowly (> 2 seconds).
Child is lethargic, abnormally sleepy, or completely unconscious.
Eyes are deeply sunken; child cannot drink or drinks eagerly/greedily.
Blood is visible in stool (Dysentery).
Vomiting everything consumed, unable to retain ORS.
doctor_referral_advice: 🚨 Severe dehydration detected: Immediately refer to PHC/FRU for intravenous (IV) Ringer Lactate fluids. Do not delay transfer.
source_citation: MoHFW Child Health IMNCI Guidelines / WHO Diarrhoea Protocol

title: High Fever Home Care & Tepid Sponging
scenario: Elevated body temperature (>38.5 C or >101.3 F) in infants, children, or pregnant women.
steps: Keep the patient in a well-ventilated, airy room with light, loose cotton clothing.
Offer plenty of oral fluids (clean water, lemon water, buttermilk, light soups) to prevent dehydration.
Perform Tepid Sponging: Use cloth soaked in lukewarm/tap water (NOT ice water). Gently sponge forehead, neck, armpits, and groin for 10-15 minutes.
If paracetamol is available per standing orders: administer age-weight-appropriate paracetamol syrup/tablet (10-15 mg/kg per dose, minimum 4-6 hours apart).
Monitor temperature every 2 hours.
what_not_to_do: NEVER wrap a feverish child in heavy blankets or thick woollens.
NEVER use cold ice-water or alcohol rub for sponging (causes severe shivering and temperature rebound).
NEVER give Aspirin to children or adolescents (risk of fatal Reye syndrome).
red_flags: Fever accompanied by stiff neck, altered consciousness, or inability to bend head forward.
Convulsions, fits, or abnormal jerky eye/limb movements.
Purple/dark red petechial rash on skin that does not fade under pressure.
Child breathing rapidly or chest drawing inward.
Fever lasting continuously for more than 7 days.
doctor_referral_advice: 🚨 High-risk fever red flag present: Possible meningitis, cerebral malaria, or severe pneumonia. Immediate referral to PHC Medical Officer.
source_citation: MoHFW Integrated Management of Neonatal & Childhood Illness (IMNCI)

title: Superficial Cuts, Bleeding & Animal Bites
scenario: Minor kitchen cuts, abrasions, lacerations, or dog/monkey scratches in village households.
steps: For minor bleeding cuts: Apply firm, continuous direct pressure over the wound using a clean gauze or cotton cloth for 5-10 minutes.
Clean the wound gently under running tap water and mild soap to wash out visible dirt and grit.
Apply povidone-iodine or clean sterile dressing once bleeding stops.
For ANIMAL BITES (Dog, cat, monkey): Wash immediately under running water with alkaline soap vigorously for 15 minutes minimum.
Verify Tetanus (Td) immunization status.
what_not_to_do: NEVER apply caustic lime (sunnam), chili powder, coffee powder, or mud to animal bites or bleeding cuts.
NEVER suture or close an animal bite wound primarily (traps rabies virus).
NEVER apply a tourniquet tightly around a limb unless life-threatening arterial bleeding.
red_flags: Spurting bright red blood that does not stop after 10 minutes of direct pressure (Arterial hemorrhage).
Wound caused by a wild animal or suspected rabid dog.
Deep penetrating puncture wound from rusted nails or farm tools.
Wound edges gaping open, requiring surgical sutures.
doctor_referral_advice: 🚨 For all animal bites: Immediate referral to PHC for Anti-Rabies Vaccine (ARV) and Immunoglobulin (RIG). For arterial bleeding: Call 108.
source_citation: National Rabies Control Programme (NRCP) / MoHFW First Aid Manual

title: Fainting, Dizziness & Heat Exhaustion
scenario: Sudden temporary loss of consciousness due to prolonged standing in heat, dehydration, or low blood pressure.
steps: Check responsiveness: Tap shoulder and call loudly. Check if chest is rising normally.
If breathing normally: Lay the patient flat on their back and elevate legs 30 cm (12 inches) above heart level.
Loosen tight collars, belts, and constrictive clothing.
Ensure fresh air flow. Fan the patient or move to shade.
Once fully awake and alert, offer sips of water with a pinch of salt and sugar, or ORS.
what_not_to_do: NEVER force water or medicine into the mouth of an unconscious or semi-conscious person (causes choking/aspiration).
NEVER slap the patient's face or make them stand up abruptly.
red_flags: Person remains unconscious for more than 1 minute.
Loss of consciousness preceded by chest pain, shortness of breath, or palpitations.
Patient is a pregnant mother in 2nd or 3rd trimester.
Fainting occurred with urinary incontinence, tongue biting, or rhythmic limb jerking (Seizure).
doctor_referral_advice: 🚨 If patient does not regain consciousness promptly or is pregnant: Place in recovery position (left lateral) and dial 108 immediately.
source_citation: WHO Basic Emergency Care / MoHFW First Responder Protocols

title: Choking Relief in Infants & Young Children
scenario: Sudden inability to breathe, cough, or cry after swallowing coins, seeds, marbles, or food.
steps: For INFANTS (< 1 year): Place infant face down along your forearm, supporting head with hand. Deliver 5 firm back blows between shoulder blades.
If object does not expel: Turn infant face up, give 5 quick chest thrusts with two fingers over middle of breastbone.
For CHILDREN (> 1 year): Stand behind child, wrap arms around waist, make a fist above navel, perform 5 inward-upward abdominal thrusts (Heimlich maneuver).
Repeat sequence until foreign object is dislodged or child begins coughing/crying.
what_not_to_do: NEVER perform blind finger sweeps in mouth (pushes foreign object deeper into airway).
red_flags: Child's lips, face, or fingernails turn blue/cyanotic.
Child becomes completely silent, limp, or unresponsive.
Unable to speak, cry, or make any sound.
doctor_referral_advice: 🚨 Critical airway obstruction: Shout for help immediately, call 108, and continue back blows/chest thrusts while en route to hospital.
source_citation: American Heart Association / MoHFW Pediatric First Aid Guidelines
